title: Evenings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: New federal reporting rules proposed as 55% of primary voters oppose nearby data centers.

lines.text: Good evening, and welcome to Evenings with Graham & Emmy — the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy. Tonight we start with fresh federal legislation from a West Michigan congresswoman and a poll showing most primary voters want nothing to do with these projects in their backyards.
Exactly, Emmy. U.S. Rep. Hillary Scholten introduced two bills Monday that would force data center operators to report their water and energy use every year.
Why now? We've seen months of local fights over power, water, and taxes. What does her legislation actually do?

It mandates annual surveys of resource consumption and updates Defense Department cooling standards to better protect water supplies. The goal is transparency so communities know what they're signing up for.
That sounds like it could help towns decide. But is this just federal paperwork, or could it actually slow projects here in Michigan?
It would create a national baseline. Right now siting is almost entirely local, so the bills wouldn't override townships, but the data could fuel lawsuits or stricter local rules.
Interesting. We've also got that poll from Sunday showing 55 percent of Michigan primary voters oppose data centers near them, jumping to 63 percent among likely Democrats.
Yes, and that opposition lines up with the water and rate concerns Scholten is trying to address. Voters are clearly paying attention as projects multiply.
Who are the main players pushing back locally? Townships like Saline and Lowell have been vocal.
Residents and some officials cite farmland loss, higher electric bills, and strained water systems. On the other side, utilities like DTE argue big loads help stabilize rates for everyone.
DTE said yesterday that data centers are key to holding down power rates. How does that square with the poll numbers?

The utility sees steady demand growth and wants those large customers on the grid. Critics worry the opposite: that one big campus could drive up costs for households if infrastructure upgrades get passed along.
What about Senate candidate John James? He weighed in Saturday saying let Michigan towns decide siting and taxes.
James told The Detroit News he'd keep decisions local rather than impose state rules. That stance could resonate in places like Saline Township where residents are already battling over permits.
Scholten is a Democrat from Grand Rapids pushing federal standards. James is the Republican Senate candidate favoring local control. How do those positions play with today's primary voters?
The poll shows broad skepticism, so both approaches get tested. Voters in data-center counties will see whether local control or federal guardrails feels like the better protection.
What happens next with Scholten's bills? Do they have a real shot in Congress?
They just dropped Monday, so early days. Supporters hope the reporting requirements become a model that states copy. Opponents may argue it adds red tape without solving local issues.
And the water angle feels especially relevant after Lowell's moves this week.
Exactly. We'll get to those local stories in a minute, but the bigger picture is that federal transparency could give residents the facts they say have been missing.
History-wise, Michigan has seen data centers come in quietly for years. Now the scale is different with AI demand.
Right. Earlier projects were smaller; today's proposals run hundreds of megawatts and touch multiple counties. That jump in size is why the fights feel more urgent.
So if these bills pass, would we finally get numbers on how much a typical Michigan data center pulls from the grid and aquifers?
That's the idea. Annual public data could show trends over time and let planners compare projects before approvals.
What about farmland conversion? Some residents worry prime ag land gets paved over.
The bills don't directly address land use, but better energy and water data might highlight projects that need massive new infrastructure, indirectly protecting rural areas.
And tax revenue is the carrot. Wayne County's $6 billion proposal yesterday promised thousands of construction jobs.
Yes, but locals still weigh that against long-term grid strain. The conversation always circles back to who pays if demand spikes.
What should listeners watch for in the coming weeks?
How other members of Congress react to Scholten's bills and whether the poll numbers shift after today's primary results come in.
Fair enough. Let's turn to the other stories making news this week.
Starting with today: a new report questions whether Governor Whitmer advanced a big facility in Saline Township before all local permits were locked in.
Residents in Washtenaw County could see major shifts in power demand and tax revenue. The timing puts the governor's office on the defensive right as voters head to the polls.
Also today, Lowell city officials suspended sewer and water talks with the township, halting progress on another proposed center.
That leaves Kent County residents wondering if the project can ever secure the infrastructure it needs. Signals growing pushback on resource strain.
Yesterday we saw a $6 billion campus plan land in Wayne County, promising construction jobs but heavy electricity demand.
Local officials haven't scheduled a formal review yet. Tax gains versus grid pressure will be the debate there.
Same day, the Lowell City Council ended all talks with Microsoft over secrecy concerns on power needs and impacts.
That blocks one of the bigger West Michigan projects discussed this year. Uncertainty now for jobs and rates in Kent County.
Washtenaw residents filed recall signatures against seven officials over data center fights.
The effort targets power, water, and tax issues. Voters thirty miles away will watch if those recalls reach the ballot.
DTE's filing yesterday tied future rate stability to securing large data center loads.
Their project pipeline stays steady even as forecasts rise. Households could feel it in bills either way.
And on Saturday, Hyperscale Data shifted power at its Dowagiac site from Bitcoin to a 20-megawatt AI deal worth over a billion dollars long term.
Residents are still litigating noise complaints from the facility. The switch shows how these sites can pivot uses quickly.
No major public meetings on the calendar for tonight or tomorrow that we've confirmed yet.
Listeners should check the Michigan Data Center Tracker for any last-minute additions.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Scholten's Federal Data Center Bills Meet Michigan Voter Pushback
